I am 65 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou for more than forty years. I know this land, and I know what works here on the North China Plain. The winters are cold, the summers are hot and rainy, and the groundwater is deep but still reachable. I do not chase fads. I plant what feeds my family and what I can sell reliably to the grain station.

My wheat is already in the ground—I sowed it last October after the National Day holiday, as I always do. I grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation on the same plots. This year I have seven mu that I will manage this way. The wheat variety I use is Luyuan 502, an improved variety that my neighbors and I have trusted for years. It stands up well to the dry spring winds here and gives steady yields. For the maize that will follow the wheat in June, I will plant Denghai 605, a hybrid seed. The yield is good and the grain dries well before autumn.

At my age, I do not waste energy on unnecessary ploughing. I rotary-tilled the wheat fields before sowing last autumn, which is what most of us do here. For the maize, I will use no-tillage after the wheat comes off—I have learned that planting directly into the stubble saves time, keeps moisture in the soil during the hot June days, and still gives me a good crop.

Fertilizer is the most important thing after water. For the wheat, I will put down about 45 jin of nitrogen fertilizer per mu, split between basal dressing and the spring topdressing at green-up. I also spread compound fertilizer to give the crop some phosphorus and potassium, because the soil here is tired after so many years of wheat. For the maize, I fertilize a bit less on the nitrogen, around 35 to 40 jin per mu, but I make sure it gets enough during the big growth period in July.

Water is life. The wheat needs three good irrigations: the overwinter water, the jointing water in spring, and one more at heading or grain-filling if the sky gives us no rain. The maize needs two irrigations, usually right after sowing to help it emerge, and again at the big flare stage if July turns dry.

I spray pesticides about four times on the wheat—there are aphids, rust, and weeds that will ruin everything if you let them. For the maize, three applications are usually enough, mainly for armyworm and weeds. I watch the fields every morning. If I see damage, I spray. If not, I wait.

I expect my wheat to yield about 500 kg per mu this year if the spring drought does not hit too hard. The maize should give me about 550 kg per mu if the summer rains come on time. These are honest, realistic numbers—not the inflated promises on seed packets, but what this soil actually gives me.
